n: After Korihor’s end, Alma hears that the Zoramites, led by a man named Zoram, are worshipping lifeless idols and twisting the Lord’s ways. Once again his heart aches over sin among his people.
Alma feels deep sorrow, not just at their sin but at the split itself. The Zoramites had broken away from the Nephite community.
Mormon locates Antionum: east of Zarahemla near the sea, south of Jershon, bordering a wilderness full of Lamanites. That position made the Zoramites strategically important.
The Nephites feared the Zoramites would ally with the Lamanites. That fear later proved true, as the Zoramites joined the Lamanites in war.
A key principle: preaching God’s word had changed people more powerfully than the sword or anything else. So Alma decides to try “the virtue of the word”—its power—rather than force.

f.w: the virtue of the word of God
f.g: Virtue here means power or effectiveness.

n: Alma assembles a strong team: three of the sons of Mosiah (Himni stays to lead the church in Zarahemla), Amulek and Zeezrom from Melek, and two of his own sons.
His eldest son Helaman stays home; Shiblon and Corianton go with him. Alma later gives each son personal counsel in chapters 36–42.
Because the Zoramites had once been Nephites, they had already been taught the gospel. Their problem was not ignorance but turning away.

f.g: People who broke away from a group and its beliefs.

n: They had stopped keeping the commandments and the law of Moses.
They also abandoned daily prayer—the very habit that guards against temptation.

f.w: that they might not enter into temptation

n: In short, they had distorted the Lord’s ways in many respects, so Alma’s team goes to call them back.
The missionaries are amazed. The Zoramites have synagogues and meet one day a week they call “the day of the Lord,” but their worship is unlike anything Alma has seen.

f.g: Meeting houses for worship and teaching.

n: In the center of each synagogue stands a tall platform, so high that it is above a person’s head and so narrow at the top that only one person fits.
Each worshipper climbs up, raises his hands to heaven, and shouts the same words aloud—a public show of religion.
The Zoramite prayer begins. They describe God as a spirit only, now and forever—denying that God has a body or could come to earth as Christ.
They thank God for making them better than others, scorn their brethren’s beliefs as childish, claim to be uniquely chosen, and declare there will be no Christ.

f.g: Chosen. They believed God had predetermined them alone for salvation.

n: They use true words (“the same yesterday, today, and forever”) to support a false idea: they alone are chosen while everyone else is destined for hell. They even thank God for freeing them from belief in Christ.

f.w: the same yesterday, today, and forever

n: The prayer ends by praising themselves as a chosen, holy people. It echoes the Pharisee in Jesus’ parable who thanked God he was not like others.

f.w: a chosen and a holy people

n: Alma and his companions are stunned beyond words by what they hear.
Every single worshipper climbs up and repeats the identical prayer, word for word.
The platform is called the Rameumptom, which Mormon translates as “the holy stand.”

f.g: A Nephite-era name the text interprets as “the holy stand.”

n: Mormon summarizes the prayer’s theme: gratitude for being chosen and for not believing in “things to come”—that is, in a future Christ, the same argument Korihor made.
Afterward they go home and never mention God again until the next week. Their religion is a once-a-week ritual with no effect on daily life.

f.w: never speaking of their God again

n: Alma is grieved. Behind the ritual he sees hearts fixed on gold, silver, and fine goods.
Their pride shows in their boasting.
Alma begins his own prayer—a striking contrast to the Rameumptom. He asks how long God’s servants must live amid such open wickedness.
He notes the irony: they pray with their mouths, but their hearts are swallowed up in pride and worldly things.

f.w: cry unto thee with their mouths

n: Alma describes their expensive clothes, curled hair, bracelets, and gold. Their hearts are set on these things even as they thank God they alone are chosen.

f.g: Curls of hair, a sign of costly grooming.

n: Worst of all, they claim God has revealed to them that there will be no Christ.
Alma pleads for strength. He admits his own weakness and says their wickedness causes him real pain.
He asks God to comfort his soul “in Christ”—the very Being the Zoramites deny—and to help him bear patiently the trials ahead.
Alma then prays for each of his companions by name, asking God to comfort them in Christ and give them success.
He asks that they all have strength to endure the trials this mission will bring.
His real goal is clear: to bring the Zoramites back to God through Christ.
The heart of the prayer: these souls are precious, and many are family. Alma asks for power and wisdom to win them back, showing love even for people he has just criticized.
Alma lays his hands on his companions, and they are filled with the Holy Spirit.

f.g: Placed his hands on them, as in a blessing.

n: The missionaries split up to cover more ground, not worrying about food, drink, or clothing—trusting God as Jesus later taught His disciples.
The Lord answers Alma’s prayer: they do not go hungry or thirsty, and any suffering is swallowed up in the joy of Christ—because Alma prayed in faith.

f.w: swallowed up in the joy of Christ
